title: CCPA & California Privacy for Beginners: Complete Guide
metaDescription: Learn CCPA basics, your California privacy rights, and how to opt out of data sales. Simple guide for consumers and businesses.
intro: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) gives California residents powerful rights over their personal data. This guide explains your privacy rights, how to exercise them, and what businesses must do to comply with California privacy law.
prerequisites: Be a California resident or business serving California customers
Basic understanding of what personal data is
Access to email for making privacy requests

steps.title: Understand Your CCPA Rights
steps.description: The CCPA started with four core privacy rights. The CPRA later added the right to correct and the right to limit use of sensitive personal information, covered in the next step.
actions: Right to know what personal information is collected about you
Right to delete personal information held by businesses
Right to opt out of the sale of your personal information
Right to non-discrimination for exercising your privacy rights
steps.proTip: These rights apply to businesses that collect data from California residents, even if the business is located outside California.

steps.title: Learn the Difference Between CCPA and CPRA
steps.description: The California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA) expanded CCPA with additional protections starting January 2023.
actions: Coverage starts at $25M+ revenue (adjusted to $26,625,000) or 100,000+ consumers or households; the CPRA raised that count from 50,000
CPRA adds right to correct inaccurate information
CPRA creates new category for 'sensitive personal information'
CPRA establishes the California Privacy Protection Agency
steps.proTip: CPRA is essentially CCPA 2.0 - it builds on the original law rather than replacing it.

steps.title: Identify Which Businesses Must Comply
steps.description: Not all businesses are subject to CCPA. Learn which companies must follow California privacy law.
actions: Annual gross revenue over $25 million, adjusted for inflation to $26,625,000 since January 1, 2025
Buy, sell, or share personal info of 100,000+ consumers or households annually
Derive 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information
Any business that meets one of these three criteria
steps.warning: Even small businesses may be covered if they handle large amounts of personal data or generate significant revenue from data sales.

steps.title: Make a 'Do Not Sell My Info' Request
steps.description: Exercise your right to opt out of the sale of your personal information using these methods.
actions: Look for 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' links on websites
Submit requests through company privacy pages or contact forms
Send email requests to privacy contact addresses
Turn on Global Privacy Control in your browser so sites receive an opt-out automatically (Brave and DuckDuckGo send it by default; Firefox has a setting)
steps.proTip: Businesses must act on an opt-out request within 15 business days and cannot ask why you're making it.

steps.title: Request Access to Your Personal Information
steps.description: Use your right to know what personal information companies have collected about you.
actions: Submit requests through company websites or privacy portals
Include your full name, contact information, and specific request details
Ask for the past 12 months, and for personal information collected on or after January 1, 2022 you can ask beyond that window too
Ask for categories of data, sources, and third parties who received it
steps.proTip: Companies have 45 days to respond and may request additional information to verify your identity.

steps.title: Request Deletion of Your Personal Information
steps.description: Exercise your right to have businesses delete the personal information they've collected about you.
actions: Submit deletion requests through official company channels
Verify your identity as required by the business
Understand that some information may be retained for legal reasons
Follow up if you don't receive confirmation within 45 days
steps.warning: Businesses can keep some data for legal compliance, fraud prevention, or to complete transactions you initiated.

steps.title: Understand Business Compliance Requirements
steps.description: If you're a business owner, learn the basic steps to comply with CCPA requirements.
actions: Update your privacy policy to include CCPA disclosures
Add 'Do Not Sell' links to your website
Establish processes to handle consumer requests
Train employees on CCPA requirements and response procedures
steps.proTip: Consider using privacy management platforms to automate request handling and ensure compliance.

pro_tips: Keep records of all privacy requests you make, including dates and company responses for your protection.
Block third-party cookies in your browser settings to reduce the cross-site tracking that feeds data sales and ad profiles.
Review privacy policies regularly as companies update their data practices and CCPA disclosures.
Set up Google Alerts for your name to monitor when your personal information appears online.
Consider using data broker opt-out services to remove your information from people-search websites.

faqs.question: Does CCPA apply to me if I don't live in California?
faqs.answer: The CCPA covers California residents, and the law borrows the state's tax definition of residency, so a visit does not make you a consumer under it. Some companies extend CCPA rights to all users regardless of location.

faqs.question: Can companies charge me for exercising my CCPA rights?
faqs.answer: No, companies cannot charge fees for processing CCPA requests or discriminate against you for exercising your privacy rights. This includes not denying services or charging different prices.

faqs.question: How long do businesses have to respond to my CCPA request?
faqs.answer: Businesses must confirm receipt within 10 business days and provide a complete response within 45 calendar days. They can extend by 45 more days if needed, but must notify you of the extension.

faqs.question: What's the difference between 'selling' and 'sharing' personal information?
faqs.answer: Under CCPA, 'selling' means exchanging personal info for money. 'Sharing' (added by CPRA) includes giving data to third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising, even without payment.

faqs.question: Can I sue a company for CCPA violations?
faqs.answer: You can only sue for data breaches involving unencrypted personal information. Other CCPA violations are enforced by the California Attorney General and Privacy Protection Agency, not through private lawsuits.
